question: My crossbred dairy cow gives 8 litres a day but used to give 12. She looks thinner and it is the dry season. What should I check and change in her feeding?
answer: A drop in yield with weight loss in the dry season usually means energy and protein intake fell below what she needs, but rule out disease first. Check: body condition, appetite, rumen fill, mastitis (clots or hot quarters), lameness, worm burden, and whether she is pregnant far along. On feeding, forage is the foundation. If pasture is dry and fibrous, she is eating low-protein roughage and losing condition. Practical steps: (1) offer conserved forage such as hay or silage, plus any Napier, sweet potato vines, or legume fodder like calliandra or desmodium for protein; (2) supplement with dairy meal roughly matched to yield, split across milkings, without dumping large amounts at once; (3) ensure free access to clean water and mineral lick or dicalcium phosphate, since water restriction alone cuts milk sharply; (4) deworm on veterinary advice and control ticks. Change feed gradually over a week to avoid acidosis. If she does not improve within two to three weeks of better feeding, call a veterinary officer.

question: My calf has swollen glands near the ear and shoulder, high fever and will not feed. Neighbours say East Coast Fever. What do I do?
answer: Swollen parotid and prescapular lymph nodes with high fever in a tick-exposed calf is a classic East Coast Fever presentation, caused by Theileria parva and spread by the brown ear tick. This is an emergency. Call a veterinary officer or animal health worker today, because treatment with the specific drugs works best when started early and the case fatality rate is high once breathing becomes difficult. While you wait: move the calf to shade, offer water, and do not self-medicate with random antibiotics, which do not treat Theileria. Prevention going forward is tick control on a strict schedule with acaricide spray or dip, keeping the ears and tail regions well covered, plus the infection and treatment method vaccination where it is available in your district. Do not share needles between animals.

question: Many of my local chickens died suddenly. They had greenish droppings and twisted necks before dying. What was it and how do I protect the rest?
answer: Sudden high mortality with greenish diarrhoea and nervous signs such as twisted neck strongly suggests Newcastle disease, which is common and devastating in village flocks. There is no cure once birds are sick. Protect the remaining flock now: (1) vaccinate healthy birds with a thermostable Newcastle vaccine, such as the I-2 strain used in village poultry programmes, following the schedule your extension or veterinary officer gives; (2) isolate sick birds away from healthy ones; (3) do not sell or give away birds from an outbreak flock; (4) dispose of carcasses by deep burial or burning, not by throwing them in the bush; (5) clean and disinfect the housing, feeders and drinkers. Going forward, vaccinate on a routine schedule, usually repeated a few times a year, and avoid mixing new birds without a quarantine period.

question: My layers started laying thin-shelled eggs and some break in the nest. What causes this?
answer: Thin or soft shells usually trace to calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D3 shortage, heat stress, ageing hens, or disease. Check in this order: (1) Feed. Are they on a proper layer ration, not grower or a home mix that got diluted with maize? Layers need substantially more calcium than growers. Offer supplementary calcium such as crushed limestone or oyster shell in a separate container so hens can top up, ideally available in the afternoon when shells form. (2) Heat. In hot weather hens pant, which disturbs the acid balance needed for shell formation. Provide shade, ventilation, and cool clean water. (3) Age. Older hens near the end of the laying cycle naturally produce thinner shells. (4) Disease. Infectious bronchitis and Newcastle can damage shell quality; look for respiratory signs and drops in production. Also collect eggs more often and pad the nest boxes to cut breakages while you fix the cause.

question: My goats have rough coats, pale gums and some are scouring. What is the likely problem?
answer: Pale gums with rough coat and diarrhoea in goats most often points to a heavy internal parasite burden, especially Haemonchus contortus, the barber pole worm, which sucks blood and causes anaemia. Confirm anaemia by checking the inner eyelid or gum colour against a FAMACHA-style chart if your extension officer has one. Act: (1) deworm affected animals with an effective product, following the correct dose by weight rather than guessing, since underdosing drives resistance; (2) rotate to a different drug class only when advised, not every single time; (3) reduce reinfection by rotating grazing, avoiding grazing very short wet pasture in early morning, and not overstocking; (4) improve nutrition and offer minerals, since well-fed goats withstand worms better. Treat only the animals that need it rather than the whole herd every time, which slows resistance. If animals are severely anaemic or continue to scour, call a veterinary officer, as coccidiosis and other diseases look similar.

question: Should I sell my maize right after harvest or store it for three months hoping for better prices?
answer: Storing to catch a seasonal price rise can pay, but only if you account for the full cost of holding. Work through it honestly: (1) Price gap. Look at what maize fetched at harvest versus three months later over the last few seasons in your local market, not just one good year. (2) Storage losses. Weevils, mould and rodents commonly eat into the quantity and quality; poor storage can wipe out the entire price gain. (3) Cost of money. If you must borrow to cover school fees now and repay with interest, that interest may exceed the price rise. (4) Storage cost. Bags, protectant, hermetic bags, or rent. (5) Risk. Prices sometimes do not rise, especially after a good regional harvest or with imports. A common practical compromise for smallholders is to sell part of the crop immediately for urgent cash needs and store the rest properly in hermetic bags. Only store grain you have dried to safe moisture, otherwise you are storing a loss. Join a group or warehouse receipt scheme if one operates near you, as bulking usually gets a better price than selling a few bags at the farm gate.

question: Middlemen come to my farm and offer low prices. How can I get a better deal without transport of my own?
answer: Your leverage comes from information, quality and volume. (1) Know the price. Check the reference price at the nearest market and any SMS or radio market information service before the buyer arrives, so you are not negotiating blind. (2) Improve quality. Well dried, cleanly sorted, uniformly graded produce commands a premium and is easier to argue for. (3) Bulk with neighbours. A group offering several tonnes attracts buyers who will come to you and compete, while one farmer with a few bags is a price taker. (4) Do not sell in desperation. Buyers read urgency; if you can cover immediate cash needs another way, you negotiate better. (5) Consider a cooperative, aggregation centre, or contract arrangement if a reputable one exists locally. (6) Weigh honestly and insist on a scale you can see, since disputed weights are a common way value leaks. Build a reputation as a reliable supplier and buyers will return with better offers.

question: How should I use a seasonal rainfall forecast that says below-normal rains are likely?
answer: Treat a seasonal forecast as a shift in odds, not a certainty, and use it to change risk, not to gamble everything. If below-normal rains are likely: (1) Choose earlier-maturing and more drought-tolerant varieties so the crop finishes before soil moisture runs out. (2) Do not plant your entire land on the first shower; stagger planting so a false start does not destroy the whole crop. (3) Reduce plant population slightly rather than crowding, since dense stands exhaust water and produce small ears. (4) Prioritise soil moisture conservation with mulch, tied ridges, zai pits, or reduced tillage where suited. (5) Be cautious about heavy fertiliser investment on a risky planting, since unused nitrogen is wasted money if the crop fails; consider splitting applications and topping up only if rains establish. (6) Diversify with a drought-hardier crop on part of the land, and keep some cash or stored food as a buffer. Keep following updates through the season, because forecasts are revised.

question: It rained heavily once and everyone is planting. How do I know if the season has really started?
answer: A single heavy shower is often a false start, and replanting after seedlings die is expensive. Practical rule of thumb used by many extension services: wait for soil to be wet to planting depth and staying moist, typically after cumulative rain over several days rather than one storm, and plant when the pattern looks established rather than isolated. Dig down and check that moisture reaches a few centimetres below where the seed will sit. Also weigh your seed cost: if seed is expensive and you cannot afford to replant, wait a little longer; if seed is cheap and the season is short, planting slightly early may be worth the risk. Staggering planting across a few days or across plots spreads the risk. Follow your district agricultural office and local seasonal forecast rather than only following what neighbours do.

question: My tomato leaves have dark brown patches spreading fast after rain, and some fruits are rotting. What is it?
answer: Rapidly spreading dark brown lesions on leaves and stems with fruit rot in cool wet weather is typical of late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans. Early blight, which shows more as concentric target-like rings on older leaves, is a different but common problem. Late blight moves very fast and can destroy a crop in days. Act: (1) Remove and destroy severely affected plants and fruit away from the field, do not leave them in the plot. (2) Apply a fungicide registered for late blight in tomato, following the label rate and pre-harvest interval, and repeat according to label while wet conditions persist; rotate active ingredients to slow resistance. (3) Improve airflow by staking and correct spacing, and avoid overhead watering late in the day. (4) Next season, rotate away from tomato, potato and other solanaceous crops in that plot, and use clean seed or seedlings. Protect early, because fungicides work far better preventively than as a rescue once the crop is heavily infected.

question: My sukuma wiki has small holes all over the leaves and I see tiny jumping beetles. What are they and what is safe to use on a leafy vegetable I harvest weekly?
answer: Small round shot-holes with tiny jumping beetles are flea beetles. Because you harvest leaves frequently, the pre-harvest interval matters enormously; a product that is fine on maize can leave unsafe residues on a vegetable picked every few days. Prefer low-residue and cultural options: (1) keep the crop well watered and well fed, since vigorous plants outgrow flea beetle damage; (2) use floating row covers or fine netting on nursery and young plants, which is very effective; (3) remove nearby weedy brassicas that host the beetles; (4) consider approved botanical or biological options such as neem-based products where registered, observing the stated interval; (5) if you must use a synthetic insecticide, choose one specifically registered for leafy brassicas and strictly observe the pre-harvest interval on the label, and tell buyers when the crop was sprayed. Never spray a product registered only for other crops on vegetables you will sell for fresh consumption.

question: My onions rot within a few weeks of harvest. How should I cure and store them?
answer: Most post-harvest onion loss comes from harvesting too early, skipping curing, or storing in humid, poorly ventilated conditions. Steps: (1) Harvest when the tops naturally fall over and necks soften for most of the crop, and stop irrigation a couple of weeks before to firm the bulbs. (2) Cure them. Lay bulbs in a single layer in a shaded, well-ventilated place, or windrow them so the leaves shade the bulbs, for one to two weeks until the necks are tight and dry and the outer skins rustle. Curing is the step most farmers skip and it matters most. (3) Sort out thick-necked, bruised, split or diseased bulbs, which rot first and spread rot to neighbours. Use those first. (4) Store in nets or slatted crates with air circulation, raised off the floor, in a cool dry ventilated store, not in sealed polythene bags. (5) Check periodically and remove any rotting bulbs. Handle gently, because bruises are entry points for rot.

question: How do I make good compost on a small farm, and how long does it take?
answer: Compost works when you balance carbon-rich and nitrogen-rich material, keep it moist, and let it breathe. Practical method: (1) Choose a shaded spot and build a heap roughly a cubic metre or more, since small heaps do not heat properly. (2) Layer alternately: browns such as dry grass, maize stover and leaves for carbon, with greens such as fresh weeds, kitchen waste, and animal manure for nitrogen. Roughly two to three parts browns to one part greens by volume is a workable starting ratio. Chop material smaller so it breaks down faster. (3) Moisten each layer to about the wetness of a wrung-out cloth, not soaking. (4) Turn the heap every two to three weeks to add air and move outer material inwards. A well-managed heap heats up within days, and is usually ready in about two to three months; an unturned heap takes considerably longer. (5) It is ready when it is dark, crumbly, smells earthy, and you cannot recognise the original materials. Avoid adding diseased plant material, persistent weed seeds and rhizomes, or anything treated with herbicide, since some herbicide residues survive composting and damage the next crop.

question: My extension officer says my soil is acidic and I should lime. What does that mean and how much lime do I need?
answer: Acidic soil, meaning a low pH, locks up phosphorus, can release toxic aluminium that stunts roots, and reduces the response you get from fertiliser you already paid for. Legumes and their rhizobia are especially sensitive. The honest answer on rate is that you should not guess: the correct lime rate depends on your measured pH, the soil texture, and the lime quality, so it is set by a soil test and local recommendation, and it varies widely between fields. What you can act on now: (1) get a soil test through your county office, a cooperative, or a testing campaign, and ask for a lime recommendation rather than just a pH number; (2) apply agricultural lime well before planting, ideally weeks to months ahead, and incorporate it into the topsoil rather than leaving it on the surface, because lime moves very slowly downward; (3) do not apply lime and certain fertilisers in the same operation, and follow the spacing advised; (4) build organic matter with manure and compost, which buffers acidity over time; (5) re-test after a couple of seasons rather than liming blindly every year. Over-liming is also harmful, so more is not better.

question: I have a small stream and about a quarter acre of vegetables. Is drip irrigation worth it compared to watering with buckets?
answer: For a quarter acre of vegetables with a reliable water source, drip usually pays for itself through labour savings, water efficiency and better yields, but the economics depend on your crop value and how you get the water pressurised. Consider: (1) Labour. Bucket watering is the single biggest time cost for most smallholders; drip frees that time for other work. (2) Water use. Drip delivers water to the root zone and loses far less to evaporation and runoff than surface flooding, which matters if the stream is seasonal. (3) Disease. Keeping foliage dry reduces fungal disease pressure compared to overhead watering, a real benefit for tomatoes. (4) Cost. Kits sized for a quarter acre are widely available; you need either a raised tank for gravity pressure or a small pump. Gravity from an elevated tank is cheapest to run. (5) Maintenance. Filtration is essential, because stream water carries silt that clogs emitters. Budget for a filter and clean it regularly, and flush lines periodically. Start with a portion of the plot rather than converting everything at once, and confirm you have a legal right to abstract water from the stream with your local water authority.

question: My tilapia in a small earthen pond grow very slowly. What are the usual reasons?
answer: Slow tilapia growth in smallholder ponds almost always comes down to overcrowding, poor feeding, poor water quality, or uncontrolled breeding. Check each: (1) Stocking density. Too many fish for the pond size and feed means everyone stays small. (2) Uncontrolled breeding. Mixed-sex tilapia breed continuously and the pond fills with stunted fingerlings competing for feed. Using all-male, sex-reversed fingerlings from a reputable hatchery is the single biggest fix for this problem. (3) Feed. Fish need consistent quality feed with adequate protein, fed in measured amounts once or twice daily at the same spot, not occasional kitchen scraps. Overfeeding fouls the water, so feed what they clear in a few minutes. (4) Water quality. Low dissolved oxygen, especially early morning, stunts growth. Watch for fish gasping at the surface at dawn, which is a warning sign. Maintain some water exchange and avoid excessive organic loading from manure. (5) Predators and poaching reduce the stock quietly. Start by getting good fingerlings and a written feeding plan, then fix density.

question: Which trees can I plant among my crops without shading them out too badly?
answer: The goal is trees that add value without competing heavily for light, water and nutrients. Favour species that are relatively open-canopied, deep-rooted, and preferably nitrogen-fixing, and manage them by pruning. Widely promoted options in East African farming systems include Grevillea robusta, which is popular on boundaries and for timber with a fairly light crown, Calliandra calothyrsus and Leucaena for fodder banks, Sesbania sesban as a fast short-term soil improver, Faidherbia albida, notable because it drops its leaves in the rainy season so it shades crops far less than most trees, and fruit trees such as mango, avocado and citrus positioned where their mature canopy will not sit over your main cropping area. Practical management matters as much as species: plant on boundaries and contours, prune side branches to lift and thin the canopy, and keep large trees away from the sunniest part of the crop field. Avoid Eucalyptus close to cropland and water sources, since it competes strongly for water. Check with your district forestry or extension officer for species released and available in your zone.

question: How do I work out whether growing tomatoes actually made me a profit last season?
answer: Profit is what remains after every cost, including the ones that do not feel like cash. Build a simple gross margin for the plot: (1) Revenue. Total quantity actually sold multiplied by the prices received, not the quantity harvested and not the price you hoped for. Note any produce lost, given away, or eaten at home separately. (2) Variable costs. Seed or seedlings, fertiliser, manure, pesticides and fungicides, hired labour, land preparation, stakes, irrigation fuel, transport, packaging, and market fees. (3) Your own labour. Count it, at least at the local wage rate, otherwise you are hiding a large cost and may conclude a crop is profitable when it is only paying you badly. (4) Subtract costs from revenue to get the gross margin for that plot and season. (5) Compare per acre against alternatives you could have grown, and against simply doing casual work. Keep a notebook through the season rather than reconstructing from memory afterwards, and keep input receipts. Repeat over several seasons, because one good or bad year is not a trend.

question: What protective equipment and precautions do I need when spraying pesticide, and what do I do with the empty container?
answer: Treat every pesticide as capable of harming you, not just the pest. Before spraying: read the label, check it is registered for that crop and pest, and mix the exact rate using a dedicated measuring container, never a kitchen cup. Wear protection: long sleeves and trousers or an overall, rubber gloves, closed shoes or boots, eye protection, and a mask or respirator suited to the product. Do not spray with bare hands, bare feet, or in shorts. During spraying: spray with the wind at your back so drift moves away from you, avoid the hottest part of the day, do not eat, drink or smoke, keep children and animals out of the field, and never blow out a blocked nozzle with your mouth. After: wash the sprayer, wash yourself thoroughly with soap, and wash your work clothes separately from family laundry. Observe the pre-harvest interval on the label before harvesting or selling, which protects your buyers and your market access. Empty containers must be triple-rinsed, with the rinse water added into the spray tank, then punctured so they cannot be reused, and disposed of as your local authority directs. Never reuse pesticide containers for water, food, or animal feed, and never store pesticide in a drink bottle.

question: Someone on my farm felt dizzy and vomited after spraying. What should I do?
answer: Treat this as a possible pesticide poisoning and act immediately. Stop exposure: move the person to fresh air, away from the sprayed area. Remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin and hair thoroughly with plenty of soap and water; if the chemical got in the eyes, rinse with clean running water for an extended period. Do not make the person vomit unless a medical professional or the label specifically instructs it, because some products cause more damage coming back up. Keep the person calm, lying on their side if drowsy, and do not give anything by mouth if they are unconscious. Get them to a health facility now, and take the pesticide container or its label with you, because the clinician needs to know the active ingredient to treat correctly. Do not wait to see if symptoms improve. Afterwards, review what went wrong, whether it was missing protective equipment, wrong mixing, spraying into the wind, or heat, and fix it before anyone sprays again.

question: How should I house dairy goats to reduce disease in a wet area?
answer: In wet areas the main enemies are damp bedding, poor ventilation and worm-contaminated ground. Build a raised slatted floor house so urine and droppings fall through, which keeps hooves dry and cuts pneumonia and footrot dramatically. Key points: raise the floor well off the ground, use slats spaced so droppings pass but hooves do not catch, provide a roof that keeps driving rain out while leaving open sides above animal height for airflow, and avoid a sealed, stuffy structure since ammonia and damp air drive respiratory disease. Give enough space per animal to prevent crowding, separate bucks, and have a place to isolate sick or newly bought animals. Clean underneath regularly and compost the manure. Provide clean water and a feed trough positioned so feed is not trampled or soiled, since worm larvae are picked up from contaminated feed and ground. Trim hooves routinely and inspect for footrot in prolonged wet weather.

question: My vegetable seedlings keep collapsing at the base in the nursery. Why?
answer: Seedlings toppling at soil level with a pinched, water-soaked stem is damping-off, caused by soil-borne fungi such as Pythium, Rhizoctonia and Fusarium. It is driven by overwatering, dense sowing, poor drainage and contaminated soil. Prevent rather than cure, because affected seedlings rarely recover. Practical measures: (1) use a well-drained nursery medium and raised seedbeds so water never stands; (2) sterilise or solarise the nursery soil before sowing, for example by covering moist soil with clear polythene in strong sun for several weeks, or use clean commercial media; (3) sow thinly, since crowded seedlings stay wet and infect each other; (4) water in the morning and only as much as needed, avoiding evening soaking; (5) provide light shade but not deep shade, as weak etiolated seedlings are more susceptible; (6) remove affected seedlings and the surrounding medium promptly. Use treated certified seed where available, and do not reuse trays without cleaning them.

question: Buyers keep rejecting part of my produce for quality. What does grading actually involve?
answer: Grading means sorting produce into consistent categories by size, colour, maturity, and freedom from defects, so a buyer knows what they are getting without inspecting every piece. Buyers reject or discount because mixed lots force them to re-sort and to price for the worst item in the bag. To grade well: (1) Learn the specific standard your buyer uses, since requirements differ between a local market, a supermarket and an export buyer; ask for it in writing if possible. (2) Sort at harvest, separating undersized, oversized, blemished, insect-damaged, cracked, over-ripe and diseased items rather than mixing them. (3) Handle gently, using crates rather than overfilled sacks, because bruising created in transport becomes the rejection you receive at the gate. (4) Pack uniformly, with clean packaging and consistent weight. (5) Sell the lower grade deliberately into a channel that accepts it, such as local processing or immediate local sale, instead of hiding it in the good lot and risking rejection of the whole consignment. Consistent graded supply is what turns a one-off buyer into a repeat buyer.

question: During very hot spells my chickens stop eating and some die. What can I do?
answer: Birds cannot sweat, so they shed heat by panting, and in hot spells feed intake falls and deaths rise, especially in heavier birds and layers. Immediate measures: (1) Water is the priority. Provide plenty of cool, clean drinking water and increase the number of drinkers so no bird has to travel or compete; refresh it often as water in the house warms quickly. (2) Improve ventilation and shade. Open sides, ensure cross-flow, use shade cloth or trees over the roof, and consider wetting the roof during the worst hours. Reduce stocking density if you can. (3) Shift feeding to the cooler parts of the day, early morning and evening, since digestion itself generates heat, and remove feed during peak heat if birds are not eating anyway. (4) Avoid handling, vaccinating, transporting or catching birds during the hottest hours. (5) Electrolyte and vitamin supplements in water during heat waves help, on advice from your veterinary or extension officer. Longer term, orient and insulate housing for heat, and choose stock suited to your climate.

question: What routine vaccinations should I plan for cattle, and does it really pay?
answer: Yes, vaccination is almost always far cheaper than treating an outbreak or losing animals. The exact schedule depends on the diseases present in your district, so the right answer comes from your district veterinary officer, but the diseases commonly covered in East African cattle programmes include foot and mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, anthrax, blackquarter, contagious bovine pleuropneumonia in some zones, brucellosis in heifers where the programme applies, and East Coast Fever through the infection and treatment method where available. Practical guidance: (1) Ask your district office for the local schedule and any government campaign dates, since some vaccinations are delivered free or subsidised during campaigns. (2) Keep a simple written record per animal with dates, so you know what is due. (3) Maintain the cold chain, because a vaccine that got warm may do nothing while giving you false confidence. (4) Vaccinate healthy animals; do not vaccinate sick or heavily stressed stock without advice. (5) Combine with tick and worm control, since parasites undermine everything else. Do not skip boosters, as a single dose without the follow-up often gives little protection.

question: I grow tomatoes in the same plot every season and yields keep falling. What rotation should I use?
answer: Continuous tomato builds up soil-borne diseases such as bacterial wilt, Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, nematodes, and blight inoculum, and depletes specific nutrients. Falling yields on the same plot is the classic signal. Rotate out of the whole solanaceous family, which includes tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant and their weedy relatives, for as long as you can manage, commonly three or more seasons for serious soil-borne problems like bacterial wilt. Rotate into unrelated families: a cereal such as maize, a legume such as beans or groundnuts which also adds nitrogen, alliums such as onion, or brassicas. Combine rotation with other measures, since rotation alone will not fix a badly infested plot: remove and destroy infected plant debris rather than ploughing it in, control volunteer solanaceous weeds, use clean certified seed or seedlings, improve drainage because bacterial wilt thrives in waterlogged soil, and consider grafted or resistant varieties where available. If bacterial wilt is confirmed, be strict, because it persists in soil for years and moves on tools, boots and water runoff.

question: My sloping plot loses topsoil every rainy season. What can I do with little money?
answer: Erosion silently removes the most fertile layer and the fertiliser you bought, so low-cost soil conservation usually returns more than most inputs. Practical low-cost measures: (1) Keep the ground covered. Mulch with crop residues or grass, and avoid leaving soil bare and finely tilled before heavy rain. Cover is the cheapest and most effective single step. (2) Work along the contour, not up and down the slope; plough, plant and ridge across the slope so each furrow catches water rather than channelling it. (3) Establish contour grass strips using vetiver, Napier or local grasses, which trap sediment and gradually build natural terraces; these cost mainly labour and planting material and can also feed livestock. (4) Dig cut-off drains above the plot to divert runoff arriving from higher land, and lead it away safely rather than into your field. (5) Plant trees and shrubs on boundaries and the steepest sections. (6) On very steep land, consider bench terraces built progressively over seasons as labour allows. Start at the top of the slope, because water arriving from above will undo work done only at the bottom.

question: My milk is sometimes rejected at the collection centre for failing the quality test. How do I fix that?
answer: Rejections usually come from bacterial contamination, added water, mastitis milk, or antibiotic residues. Work through the chain: (1) Udder health. Check for mastitis regularly, for example with a strip cup at each milking or California Mastitis Test, and keep mastitis milk out of the bulk. Milk affected cows last. (2) Milking hygiene. Wash hands and udder with clean water, dry with a clean individual cloth or paper, and milk into a clean container. (3) Equipment. Use seamless aluminium or stainless steel cans, not plastic jerricans, which are almost impossible to clean properly and are a very common cause of failure. Wash immediately after use with hot water and detergent, rinse, and dry upside down in the sun. (4) Cooling and time. Bacteria multiply fast in warm milk; deliver quickly, keep the can shaded and cool during transport, and never top up fresh milk into old milk. (5) Antibiotic residues. Observe the full withdrawal period after treating a cow, and discard her milk for the stated days; residues fail tests and can spoil an entire bulk tank, which is expensive and damages trust. (6) Never add water; it is detected and it destroys your reputation.

question: Pasture is finished and the dry season has months to run. How do I keep my cattle alive?
answer: In a worsening drought the honest priority is to protect a viable core herd rather than to keep every animal thin and at risk. Practical sequence: (1) Assess and destock early. Selling weaker, older, unproductive and surplus animals while they still have condition and while prices have not collapsed is usually better than losing them later for nothing. This is the hardest advice and the most valuable, because everyone tries to sell at the same time once animals are emaciated. (2) Prioritise feed for the core, meaning breeding females in good condition, pregnant animals and productive milkers. (3) Stretch feed with conserved hay, crop residues such as maize stover and bean haulms, and where advised, treated stover or purchased concentrate. Chop and store residues now rather than letting them be trampled. (4) Water. Reduce walking distance to water where possible, since long treks burn the energy the animals cannot spare. Keep water clean. (5) Minerals and health. Maintain vaccination and parasite control, since starved animals succumb quickly to disease. (6) Track condition scores weekly and act on the trend rather than waiting. Coordinate with your district livestock office on any emergency feed or offtake programmes.

question: When should I pick tomatoes if the market is a day away by matatu?
answer: Match ripeness to the time and handling between your field and the buyer. For a market roughly a day away with rough transport, pick at the breaker or turning stage, meaning the fruit has just started to show colour change at the blossom end but is still firm, rather than fully red. Tomatoes continue ripening after harvest, so firm turning fruit arrives in good condition and gives the trader shelf life, while fully ripe fruit bruises and arrives soft or split. Other points: harvest in the cool of early morning, not in the heat of the day; handle gently and never tip fruit from height; use ventilated crates rather than overfilled sacks, since sacks crush the bottom layers; keep harvested fruit in shade immediately rather than leaving crates in the sun while you finish picking; and sort out cracked, sunburnt and diseased fruit before packing, because one rotting fruit spoils its neighbours in transit. If you are selling for immediate local consumption instead, riper fruit is fine and often preferred.

question: My pigs grow slowly and feed is expensive. How can I reduce feed cost without stunting them?
answer: Feed is typically the largest cost in pig production, so the aim is cheaper feed per kilogram of gain, not simply less feed, since underfeeding lengthens the time to market and often costs more overall. Approaches: (1) Balance the ration rather than diluting it. Pigs need adequate protein and lysine, especially when young; cutting protein to save money slows growth disproportionately. Feed a proper starter and grower, then economise more in the finisher phase. (2) Use locally available energy and protein sources where quality can be assured, such as maize bran, sweet potato vines, brewers waste and other by-products, but introduce them gradually and be careful with bulky wet feeds for young pigs, which cannot eat enough volume. (3) Watch quality. Mouldy feed causes real losses and health problems; store feed dry and off the floor. (4) Reduce waste. Use troughs that stop pigs walking in and fouling feed, which commonly wastes a substantial share. (5) Control worms and provide clean water constantly, since parasites and water restriction quietly destroy feed conversion. (6) Keep records of feed used and weight gained so you can tell which change actually worked.

question: My groundnut plants are stunted with yellow mottled, bunched leaves. What is wrong?
answer: Stunting with bright yellow mottling and bunched, distorted foliage in groundnut is characteristic of groundnut rosette disease, a virus complex transmitted by aphids. It can cause near-total loss when it strikes early. There is no cure for infected plants, so management is preventive for the current and next crop: (1) Plant resistant varieties where they have been released for your area, which is the single most effective measure. (2) Plant early and at the recommended, relatively dense spacing, since sparse late-planted crops attract more aphids and suffer more. (3) Rogue out infected plants early to reduce the source of virus. (4) Control aphids where justified, though insecticide alone rarely rescues a badly infected crop. (5) Avoid planting next to an older infected groundnut field. Ask your extension officer or NARO for rosette-resistant varieties available locally, and use certified seed rather than recycled seed from an affected field.

question: My sweet potato roots have tunnels and taste bitter. What causes this?
answer: Tunnelled roots with a bitter taste and unpleasant smell indicate sweet potato weevil, the most serious sweet potato pest in the region. The larvae bore into roots, and even light damage makes roots bitter and unmarketable because the plant produces defensive compounds. Because the weevil reaches roots through soil cracks and exposed roots, management focuses on denying access: (1) Plant clean, weevil-free vines from a reliable source, and use the tips rather than old cuttings from an infested field. (2) Hill up soil around the plants and re-hill when cracks appear in dry weather, since cracks are the main highway to the roots. (3) Keep the crop adequately moist where possible, because drought-cracked soil greatly worsens infestation. (4) Harvest on time; leaving mature roots in the ground lets damage accumulate rapidly. (5) Practise rotation and destroy crop residues and volunteer plants after harvest, as these carry the weevil to the next crop. (6) Avoid planting new fields adjacent to old infested ones. Pheromone traps are used in some programmes for monitoring and mass trapping where available.

question: How do I reduce aflatoxin in groundnuts, which I hear is worse than in maize?
answer: Groundnuts are indeed high risk because the pods sit in the soil where Aspergillus lives, and contamination can begin before harvest, especially after end-of-season drought stress. Reduce risk across the whole chain: (1) In the field, avoid severe late-season drought stress where you can, and control pests and diseases that damage pods, since damaged pods admit the fungus. (2) Harvest at proper maturity; both immature and over-mature, delayed harvests raise risk. Avoid leaving lifted plants lying on damp soil. (3) Dry fast and correctly. Windrow with pods off the ground and turned up, or dry on raised racks and tarpaulins, never directly on bare soil, and protect from rain and night dew. Get them dry quickly rather than letting them sit damp. (4) Sort ruthlessly. Discard shrivelled, discoloured, mouldy, insect-damaged and broken kernels, which carry most of the toxin. This hand sorting step removes a large share of contamination. (5) Store dry in ventilated bags off the floor in a dry store, and never re-wet. (6) Do not feed heavily mouldy nuts to animals or press them for oil for consumption; aflatoxin is not destroyed by normal cooking or roasting. Where testing services exist, use them for anything you sell in volume.

question: What records should I keep for a small dairy herd?
answer: Records turn guesswork into decisions. Keep it simple enough that you actually maintain it. Per animal: identity and date of birth, parentage, breeding and service dates with the bull or straw used, pregnancy diagnosis result, calving dates and calf details, and disposal or death with the reason. Health: every treatment with the date, product, dose, who administered it, and crucially the milk and meat withdrawal period, so you never sell milk with antibiotic residues. Vaccination and deworming dates. Production: daily or regular milk yield per cow, which is what tells you whether a cow is worth her feed and whether a feeding change worked. Feed: what was bought, quantity, price, and what was fed. Money: milk sales and prices, input costs, veterinary costs. From these you can compute the numbers that matter, including calving interval, days open, milk per cow per lactation, and cost per litre. Use a simple exercise book or a phone app; the format matters far less than doing it consistently on the day rather than from memory at month end.

question: How do I tell certified seed from fake seed at the agro-dealer?
answer: Counterfeit seed is a real problem and it can cost you an entire season. Reduce your risk: (1) Buy from a licensed, established agro-dealer with a physical shop and a reputation to protect, not from a hawker at the roadside or the market floor. (2) Check the packaging. Genuine certified seed comes in a sealed, undamaged, professionally printed pack from a known company, with the variety name, lot or batch number, germination percentage, date of packing and expiry, and the certification tag from the national seed authority. Loose seed scooped from an open sack is not certified seed. (3) Look for the authentication feature used in your country, such as a scratch-off code you can verify by SMS, and actually send the code rather than trusting the sticker. (4) Insist on a receipt showing the shop, date, variety and lot number, which is your only recourse if the seed fails. (5) Be suspicious of prices well below the market, and of a pack that has been opened, resealed, faded, or is past its date. (6) Report suspected fakes to the seed regulator and your extension officer, since that is how counterfeit supply chains get shut down. Keep the empty pack and tag until the crop has established.

question: Should I water my kitchen garden in the morning or evening?
answer: Morning is generally the better default. Watering early gives the plants moisture before the heat of the day, and leaves that do get wet dry quickly in the morning sun, which reduces fungal disease. Evening watering leaves foliage damp through the cool night, and prolonged leaf wetness is exactly what late blight, downy mildew and many leaf spots need to infect. Midday watering is the least efficient because much is lost to evaporation before it reaches the roots, although it will not harm the plants as some believe. Two refinements matter more than the time of day: water the soil at the base rather than over the leaves, which sidesteps the disease issue entirely, and water less often but more deeply so roots grow downward, rather than a light sprinkle every day that keeps roots shallow and vulnerable. Mulch to hold what you apply. If your only free time is evening, water at the base and it is far better than not watering.

question: How soon must a newborn calf get colostrum and why does everyone insist on it?
answer: Within the first few hours, and the sooner the better. A calf is born with almost no antibodies of its own, and colostrum, the thick first milk, carries the mother's antibodies. The calf's gut can only absorb these whole antibodies for a short window that closes rapidly over the first day, so timing is everything. Practical rules: get the calf suckling within the first hour or two if possible, and certainly within the first six hours; a common guideline is a substantial feed early, roughly ten percent of body weight in colostrum across the first day, split into feeds. If the calf is weak or the dam has poor colostrum or mastitis, milk the dam and feed with a clean bottle or oesophageal tube, or use stored good-quality colostrum from another freshly calved cow. Other points: ensure the navel is dipped in iodine to prevent joint ill and navel infection, keep the calf pen clean and dry, and do not feed colostrum from a cow known to have Johne's disease or from an unverified source into a clean herd. A calf that misses colostrum is far more likely to get scours and pneumonia and to die in the first weeks, and no later treatment fully makes up for it.

question: My field flooded and stayed waterlogged for four days. Is the crop lost and what should I do now?
answer: It depends on the crop, the growth stage, the temperature and how long roots were without oxygen. Most field crops suffer badly after two to four days of full waterlogging, because roots suffocate and soil nitrogen is lost through denitrification and leaching. Assess before spending more money: (1) Check the growing point and roots. Dig up a few plants; healthy roots are firm and pale, dead roots are brown, soft and smelly. If the growing point is rotten, those plants will not recover. (2) Wait a few days of drying weather before judging, as plants often look terrible then partially recover. (3) Drain. Open channels to move standing water off the field, because every extra day compounds the damage. (4) Do not work the soil while it is saturated, as you will compact it badly and create a problem lasting seasons. (5) If a reasonable stand survives, a light nitrogen top-dress once the soil drains can help, since much nitrogen was lost, but only if the crop has enough time and root system left to use it. (6) If the stand is destroyed and the season still has enough time, consider replanting with a shorter-maturing crop. Also watch for disease, since waterlogged crops are very prone to root rots afterwards.

question: A company offered me a contract to grow for them. What should I check before signing?
answer: Contract farming can guarantee a market and inputs, but the terms decide whether it helps or traps you. Before signing: (1) Price. Is it fixed, a floor price, or tied to a market index at delivery? A fixed price protects you if the market falls and costs you if it rises; understand which risk you are taking. (2) Quality standards and rejection. Exactly what specification must you meet, who inspects, and what happens to rejected produce? Vague quality clauses are the most common source of disputes. (3) Inputs and credit. If they supply seed, fertiliser or chemicals on credit, what is the interest, how is it deducted, and what happens if the harvest fails? Understand whether you carry the loss. (4) Volume commitment. Are you obliged to deliver a set quantity, and what is the penalty if weather cuts your yield? (5) Payment terms. How many days after delivery, in what form, and what recourse exists for late payment? (6) Exit and duration. How long does it run and how can either side leave? (7) Track record. Talk to farmers who supplied them last season, not just the field officer recruiting you. Get the whole thing in writing in a language you read, keep a signed copy, and if the sums are significant, have your cooperative or a lawyer review it. Do not commit all your land to a first-time contract.

question: Can I put fresh cow manure directly on my vegetables?
answer: Better not. Fresh manure carries three problems: it can burn plants because of high ammonia and salts, it carries human pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella onto food you may eat raw, and it is full of viable weed seeds that will haunt the plot. It also releases nitrogen unpredictably. Instead: (1) Compost it properly, so the heap heats up and kills most pathogens and weed seeds, then apply the finished, dark crumbly product. (2) Or age it well and apply it to the field ahead of planting rather than to a standing food crop, incorporating it into the soil and leaving a substantial interval before harvest, particularly for anything eaten raw like salad crops. Many food safety guidelines advise a long interval, on the order of months, between raw manure application and harvest of crops eaten uncooked. (3) Never apply fresh manure as a top dressing on leafy vegetables you will harvest soon. (4) Keep manure covered while it ages so nutrients are not leached away by rain, and keep runoff out of water sources. Well-composted manure is one of the best things you can add to a vegetable plot; fresh manure on a standing salad crop is a health risk.

question: Is artificial insemination worth it for my two local cows, or should I use the neighbour's bull?
answer: Artificial insemination gives you access to genetics you could never afford to own and avoids the disease risk of a shared bull, but it demands heat detection and timely service to work. Consider: (1) Genetic gain. AI lets you use proven dairy sires to upgrade local cows, which can substantially raise milk yield in the offspring. A random neighbourhood bull gives unknown and often unimproved genetics. (2) Disease. Natural service with a shared bull spreads reproductive diseases such as brucellosis and trichomoniasis through a village; AI with properly handled semen does not. (3) Practicality. AI requires you to spot heat accurately and call the inseminator within the right window, usually serving late in standing heat. If you are away from the farm all day and cannot observe your cows, conception rates fall and repeat services cost money. (4) Access and cost. Is there a reliable inseminator who arrives promptly, and is the semen kept in proper liquid nitrogen storage? Poorly stored semen wastes your money. (5) Match the bull to your conditions. Do not choose the most extreme dairy genetics if you cannot feed the resulting animal; a crossbred that thrives on your feed base beats a high-grade cow that starves. For two cows with reliable AI service nearby and someone home to watch for heat, AI is usually the better long-term choice.

question: I want to grow vegetables year-round for steady income on half an acre. How should I plan?
answer: Steady income comes from staggered planting and matching crops to season and market, not from one big planting. Plan around: (1) Succession planting. Divide the plot into blocks and plant a portion every two to three weeks so you harvest continuously rather than facing a glut then nothing. This also protects you from a single price crash. (2) Crop mix. Combine fast-cycling leafy crops for weekly cash flow with longer-duration higher-value crops such as tomato or onion for larger payments. Do not put everything into one high-value but high-risk crop. (3) Water. Year-round production requires dry-season water. Secure it first, because a plan that collapses in the dry months is not year-round. (4) Rotation. Map which family goes into which block each cycle so you never follow tomato with tomato; write it down, because it is easy to lose track under time pressure. (5) Market first. Find out what your buyers want and when supply is thin, since the money is made by supplying when others cannot, typically in the off-season. Growing what everyone else grows at the same time guarantees the lowest price. (6) Soil. Continuous intensive cropping mines the soil; budget compost and manure into every cycle. (7) Records. Track cost and revenue per block per cycle so you learn which crops actually pay on your farm.

question: How can I tell whether my yellow, stunted maize is from striga, nitrogen shortage, or waterlogging?
answer: They look similar from the roadside but the pattern and the details differ. Nitrogen deficiency: yellowing starts on the older, lower leaves and forms a V shape from the leaf tip along the midrib, the whole field is usually affected fairly evenly or worse where soil is poorest, and the plants are pale but otherwise normal in shape. Striga: look at the ground. Purple-flowered witchweed plants emerge near the maize stems, damage appears in patches that recur in the same parts of the field year after year, affected maize is severely stunted and scorched-looking out of proportion to the soil fertility, and pulling up a maize plant may reveal striga attached to the roots. Striga is also worse on poor soils, so the two often occur together. Waterlogging: affected areas follow the low spots, drainage lines and compacted headlands rather than being uniform, yellowing appears after heavy rain, roots are brown and may smell, and plants may wilt paradoxically in wet soil because damaged roots cannot take up water. Practical check: dig in two or three places, inspect roots, walk the field to map whether the pattern follows topography, fertility, or recurring patches, and look specifically for emerged striga at the base of plants.
